title: Man subdued at Anicinabe Park identified, prompting First Nation leaders to call for 'accountability'
article: The picture of what happened at Anicinabe Park last week has become clearer, but according to some, the biggest question remaining is what will happen next.
Around noon on Tuesday, June 25, a man since identified as 57-year-old Bruce Wallace Frogg from the Wawakapewin First Nation, arrived at the Anicinabe Park general store and office in Kenora.

According to Susan Evenden, the store's manager, Frogg " was clearly having some kind of mental health issues, was angry, talking a lot, shouting a lot, and and may have poured a flammable substance around the outside of the store."

While the lone staff working at the store was able to escape safely, Frogg lit the building on fire, prompting a response by the Ontario Provincial Police (OPP), who arrived on the scene around 12:40 p.m.

In a video that circulated on social media, Frogg can be seen standing next to the on-fire store wielding two knives, seemingly brandishing them at the police forming a perimeter in and around the parking lot.
According to Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU), which has now invoked its mandate and taken over the investigation of the incident, one OPP officer ended up shooting Frogg.
After being shot, Frogg was subsequently transported to the hospital, where he was eventually pronounced deceased. No one else was injured as a result of the incident.
Local firefighters, meanwhile, were able to extinguish the blaze, but the storefront and office were burnt well past the point of being salvageable, and the building is now in ruins.
According to the SIU, t hree investigators and two forensic investigators have been assigned to the case, and Frogg's post-mortem was scheduled for Saturday, June 29.
Since the SIU announced it was launching an investigation into the matter, it has not provided any further updates or findings.

The Detachment Commander for the Kenora OPP, Insp. Jeff Duggan, has made it clear that because the SIU has invoked its mandate, he is prohibited from talking about or addressing the matter any further.

In the wake Frogg's passing, his home community of Wawakapewin was the first to express condolences on Wednesday, June 26, when the band office put out a media release commemorating his "sudden passing."

"Bruce can be remembered by his teachings and stories about the land. He was an avid outdoorsman harvesting from its bounty and sharing with family and community members," the Wawakapewin media release stated.
According to the media release, "his daughters in Wunnumin Lake First Nation are left behind to mourn the loss of their loved one."
Notably, he will also leave behind several other Froggs who are central to Wawakapewin, and he was also related to the community's former Chief Simon Frogg.

On June 28, three days after the initial incident, Grand Council Treaty #3 and Nishnawbe Aski Nation (NAN) leaders - Grand Chiefs Francis Kavanaugh and Alvin Fiddler - officially called "for accountability after (the) tragic shooting."

"On behalf of Nishnawbe Aski Nation and Grand Council Treaty #3, we extend our most heartfelt condolences and sympathy to the family and friends of Bruce Frogg and the entire community of Wawakapewin First Nation," the leaders wrote via media release.
"This tragedy has sent shockwaves through our many communities, and we are doing our best to support our members as they grieve this terrible loss."

According to GCT3 and NAN, " investigations such as the one being undertaken by Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU) are often narrow in scope, focusing on the specific actions taken by police at one particular point in time, and may not fully consider the many significant and broader systemic issues."
"Too many confrontations with police end with violence to First Nations, and our leaders are frustrated and angry," the GCT3 and NAN leaders wrote.
"There is an increasing demand for accountability when our members are harmed by police during alterations in urban centres across northwestern Ontario."

"We are already concerned with some of the things we are hearing about this fatal shooting, and this tragedy has once again raised serious questions about the conduct of the police and their interactions with First Nations peoples," Kavanaugh and Fiddler continued.
"We expect a full accounting of exactly what happened, and we will hold the appropriate people and agencies accountable for their actions."

That same day, neighbouring Kiiwetinoong Member of Provincial Parliament (MPP) Sol Mamakwa issued a statement of his own, saying Frogg's family " deserves a clear and honest explanation and investigation by the SIU."
"This incident has left us and surrounding First Nations heartbroken and grieving," Mamakwa wrote.

"It appears to be another situation where the lack of proper mental health support leads to unnecessary loss of life. Too often, First Nations people are not treated with the same care by police as others. We must all come together to ensure that it does not happen again."
The SIU is urging anyone who may have information about the incident, including video or photos, to contact the lead investigator at 1-800-787-8529.
A vigil was held for Bruce Frogg at Anicinabe Park on July 2.
